scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

While the intention behind lying to your brother about having a disorder is to help him feel less alone and more accepting of his own condition, it's not the most effective or honest approach. Here's why:

1. **Lying can damage trust**: If your brother were to discover that you've been lying to him about having Aspberger's, it could damage the trust between you two, which is essential for your close relationship.
2. **It's not a sustainable solution**: Maintaining a lie for the rest of your life can be emotionally exhausting and may lead to feelings of guilt, anxiety, or stress.
3. **It may not address the underlying issues**: Your brother's denial and shame about his condition may stem from deeper issues, such as societal stigma, fear of being perceived as different, or concerns about his future. Lying about having the condition yourself may not address these underlying concerns.
4. **There are alternative ways to support your brother**: Instead of lying, you could continue to have open and honest conversations with your brother about his condition, emphasizing that it's nothing to be ashamed of and that you're there to support him. You could also explore resources and support groups together, which may help him feel more connected to others who share similar experiences.

A more effective approach might be to:

1. **Encourage self-acceptance**: Help your brother understand that his condition is a part of who he is, and that it's not something to be ashamed of.
2. **Foster a supportive environment**: Create a safe and supportive space where your brother feels comfortable discussing his feelings and concerns.
3. **Explore resources and support**: Look into resources, such as therapy, support groups, or online communities, that can help your brother connect with others who share similar experiences and challenges.

By being honest, supportive, and understanding, you can help your brother develop a more positive and accepting relationship with his condition, without feeling the need to resort to lying.
